description_full: KBR, Inc. provides scientific, technology, and engineering solutions to governments and commercial customers worldwide. The company operates through Government Solutions and Sustainable Technology Solutions segments. It offers research and development, advanced prototyping, acquisition support, systems engineering, cyber analytics, space domain awareness, test and evaluation, data analytics and integration, systems integration and program management, global supply chain management, operations readiness and support, and professional advisory services, as well as command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance services to defense, intelligence, space, aviation, and other programs and missions for military and other government agencies. The company also operates portfolio of various proprietary process technologies for ammonia/syngas, chemical/petrochemicals, clean refining, and circular process/circular economy solutions. In addition, it provides synergistic services, including energy security, broad-based energy transition and net-zero carbon emission solutions, high-end engineering, design and program management centered around decarbonization, energy efficiency, and environmental impact and asset optimization, as well as digitally-enabled operating and monitoring solutions. KBR, Inc. was founded in 1901 and is headquartered in Houston, Texas.

Stock-based compensation of $583 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 31× revenue per employee (elevated relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: KBR, Inc. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $4.5B market cap on $7.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 15% against a 7% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 11% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $515M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.34× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.9×.

Management returns a meaningful 9.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

val: The stock trades 55% below its DCF fair value of $79.15, a meaningful margin of safety.

Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 56% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 11.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $44.86 on average, 26% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 15% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.19).
It runs a 11% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.34x.
ROE of 28% is amplified by 4.4x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.

hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.2x net debt to EBITDA ($500.0M of cash against $2.6B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.9x.
Goodwill makes up 41% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.9% over 3 years, 6.2% over 5 years and 4.3% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 25% of profits supports about 3.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 8.2% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.94 (orders lagging sales) and a backlog worth 1.7x annual revenue.
Capex runs only 0.2x depreciation (0.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 13, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.2%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only bought over the past year (4 purchases, net $945K bought).
It returns 9.2% a year to shareholders (7.3% in buybacks and 1.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 18 consecutive years, raising it 9.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 36,000 employees, each generates about $216K of revenue, 0.6x the Industrials median, and revenue has fallen 2.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $14K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $6.7M (31x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
